d: A state of motor and mental inactivity with a partial suspension of sensibility
ety: From Latin torpor (“numbness”), from torpeō (“to be numb”).
s: He fell into a deep torpor.

d: Marriage within one’s own tribe or group as required by custom or law
ety: From endo- + -gamy; compare inmarriage.
s: Endogamy historically predominated in Jewish populations, giving rise to a high prevalence of genetic diseases.

d: The occurrence of a water flow resulting from sudden rain or melting snow
ety: From Old French freschete, a diminutive of fres (“fresh”) via its feminine form fresche.
s: Between the curbs and the snow banks a freshet of clear blue water rises. Within me a freshet that chokes the narrow gorge of my veins.

d: Engrave by means of dots and flicks
ety: Probably from Dutch stippel (“small dot”), originally applied to the dots themselves and later to the technique.
s: Outside the car window was a glaze of darkness stippled with the gold of infrequent mysterious lights.

d: A covered walkway (as in a cloister)
ety: From Latin ambulatorius. By surface analysis, ambulate + -ory, or, by surface analysis, ambulator + -y.
s: It has an ambulatory and seven chapels.

d: A negotiation between enemies
ety: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk; to speak”), from Late Latin parabolō, from Latin parabola (“comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παρά (pará, “beside”) with βολή (bolḗ, “throwing”). Doublet of palaver.
s: We yield on parley, but are stormed in vain.

d: Warranting only temporal punishment
ety: From Old French venial, borrowed from Late Latin veniālem (“pardonable”), from Latin venia (“forgiveness”).
s: His venial youthful indiscretions.

d: A formal expression of praise
ety: From French panégyrique, from Ancient Greek πανηγυρικός (panēgurikós).
s: The painter's absurd fits of jealousy, his wild devotion, his extravagant panegyrics, his curious reticences—he understood them all now, and he felt sorry.

d: Proceeding to a conclusion by reason or argument rather than intuition
ety: Borrowed from Middle French discursif, formed from the stem of Latin discursus and the suffix -if, and in part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus. By surface analysis, discourse + -ive.
s: This means, at times, long and perhaps overly discursive discussions of other taxa.

d: A loyal supporter
ety: ] From Italian giannizzaro, possibly via Middle French ianissaire or Spanish jenízaro, from Ottoman Turkish یڭیچری (yeñiçeri) (whence Modern Turkish yeniçeri), from یڭی (yeñi, “new”) + چری (çeri, “soldier”). Compare Dutch janitsaar, German Janitschar. The word is attested from the early 16th century in English; the janissaries themselves date from the 14th century.
s: Every politician has a following of janissaries.

d: Feeling an inappropriate lack of seriousness
ety: Coined in 1564, from Latin levitās (“lightness, frivolity”), from levis (“lightness (in weight)”). Cognate to lever, and more distantly, light.
s: An attempt to inject a little levity into the proceedings.

d: Convex on both sides; shaped like a lentil
ety: Inherited from Middle English lenticular, lenticuler, borrowed from Medieval Latin lenticulāris (“lentil-shaped”), from Latin lenticula, from lēns + -cula, ultimately from Latin lēns (“lentil”).
s: But establishment on the fringes of everyday practice doesn't mean lenticular photography is a failure. On the contrary, the process manifests resounding cultural success through its longevity.

d: Deprive of possessions
ety: From Medieval Latin expropriātus.
s: When you have resigned, or rather consigned, your expropriated will to God, and thereby entrusted him to will for you, all his dispensations towards you are, in effect, the acts of your own will.

d: Foolishly fond of or submissive to your wife
ety: Borrowed from Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife”), from uxor (“wife”) + -ious.
s: In truth, Richard was a fond—almost an uxorious husband.

d: Of an appropriate or pertinent nature
ety: Borrowed from French à propos (“on that subject”). Similar in meaning and form, and to some extent etymology, to appropriate, but not a doublet of it.
s: Served outside the shell and sliced in bite-sized pieces, it's as apropos for a first date as a business dinner.

d: A framework that supports climbing plants
ety: Borrowed from Italian pergola, from Latin pergula.
s: While both pergolas and arbors are most dramatic cloaked in climbing, flowing plants, only a pergola will stand naked as a piece of architecture.

d: An event that is experienced as indicating important things to come
ety: From augur + -y, or from Middle English augurie, from Old French augurie, from Latin augurium.
s: Evidently he did not mean to be a mere figurehead, but to carry on the old tradition of Wilsthorpe's; and that was considered to be a good thing in itself and an augury for future prosperity.

d: Someone who performs the duties of an attendant for someone else
ety: From Middle English servitour, borrowed from Latin servītor, from servīre (“to serve”).
s: 1884, W.S. Gilbert, Princess Ida You'll find no sizars here, or servitors / or other cruel distinctions meant to draw / a line 'twixt rich and poor

d: Excessive but superficial compliments given with affected charm
ety: Borrowed from Latin unctiō.
s: To be heir, and to be king / By sacred unction, thy deserved right.

d: An outsider who seeks power or success presumptuously
ety: From carpetbag + -er, because many carried their belongings in cheap luggage made from carpet fabric.
s: “You are way behind the times,” he said. “There is no Klan in Atlanta now. Probably not in Georgia. You’ve been listening to the Klan outrage stories of your Scallawag and Carpetbagger friends.”

d: Not worth considering
ety: From Middle Low German paltrig (“ragged, rubbishy, worthless”), from palter, palte (“cloth, rag, shred”), from Old Saxon *paltro, *palto (“cloth, rag”), from Proto-Germanic *paltrô, *paltô (“scrap, rag, patch”). Of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *polto- (“cloth”), see also Proto-Slavic *poltьno (“linen”). Cognate with Low German palterig (“ragged, torn”), dialectal
s: Could someone hope to survive on such a paltry income?

d: Having a grey or brown streak or a pattern or a patchy coloring; used especially of the patterned fur of cats
ety: An alteration of brinded, probably by association with speckled, grizzled etc.
s: And there, in the middle of it was the man himself—his face twisted like a lost soul in torment, and his great brindled beard stuck upwards in his agony.

d: Regulating or controlling expenditure or personal behavior
ety: From Latin sūmptuārius (“of or relating to expenditure, sumptuary; person in charge of household expenses”) + English -ary (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Sūmptuārius is derived from sūmptus (“charge, cost, expense”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives); and sūmptus from sūmō (“to catch, seize, take; to acquire, get, obtain; to apply, employ, use; to consume, spend”) (fr
s: Sumptuary laws discouraging construction of large houses on small plots.

d: Struck with fear, dread, or consternation
ety: From Middle English agast, agasted, past participle of agasten (“to terrify”), from Old English a- (compare with Gothic 𐌿𐍃- (us-), German er-, originally meaning "out") + gæstan (“to terrify, torment”): compare Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (usgaisjan, “to terrify”, literally “to fix, to root to the spot with terror”); akin to Latin haerere (“to stick fast, cling”). By surface analysis, a- + ghast/gast. See ga
s: I was aghast when the incident unfolded in front of me.

d: Overbearing pride or presumption
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὕβρις (húbris, “insolence, sexual outrage”).
s: Antitrust prosecutors target big companies that exude hubris.

d: Cause to be confused emotionally
ety: Fanciful variant of discompose, discomfit, etc., originally discombobricate. The -bob- interfix may come from bobbery, meaning “commotion, noise”. First attested in 1834 in the United States.
s: The notes zigzag in his pieces and discombobulate the ear, just as in 12-tone works.

d: Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners
ety: From rake (“man habituated to immoral conduct”) + -ish.
s: If rakish dukes were one's thing.

d: A state of extreme poverty
ety: Inherited from Middle English privacioun, from Middle French privation, privacion, from Old French privacion, from Latin prīvātiō; compare French privation. See private.
s: Mr. McCarthy wrote for many years in relative obscurity and privation.

d: A medieval coat of chain mail consisting of metal rings sewn onto leather or cloth
ety: From Middle English brigandyn, brigantien, attested by 1456 (eventually displacing the slightly earlier synonym brigander), from Old French brigandine, from brigand + -ine.
s: Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines.

d: Showing a cheerful willingness to do favors for others
ety: From French complaisant (“willing to please”), from complaire, from Latin complacēre (“please well”), from com- (“with”) + placeō (“please”).
s: Replay our conversation You threw your accusations I'm always so complaisant I never change the station

d: Engage in boisterous, drunken merrymaking
ety: From Old French rustre, from Latin rusticus. Doublet of rustic.
s: He loved Rick and gave the best years of his life, now to roistering with him, now to hanging on to his coat-tails.

d: A medieval book (usually illustrated) with allegorical and amusing descriptions of real and fabled animals
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia (“beast, animal”). By surface analysis, beast + -ary.
s: Back in the 60s, Robin Boyd told us how ugly Australian architecture was. As his valediction, he has left us a bestiary of ugly Australians.

d: Rub elbows with
ety: From hob and nob, hob or nob (“a phrase spoken when making a toast, possibly meaning ‘give and take’; to take turns toasting or buying rounds of drinks”) (archaic), from dialectal hab nab (“to have or have not, in the sense of an invitation to have a drink”), from Old English habban (“to have, possess”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grab, seize”)) + nabban (“to not have”) (from n
s: His favorite spot in the club was the bar, where he could hobnob with the big-wigs.

d: A flattering commendation (especially when used for promotional purposes)
ety: From puff + -ery.
s: Harvest was promptly pegged as a "lite" group, a purveyor of pop puffery.

d: A loud bombastic declamation expressed with strong emotion
ety: From Middle English arang and French harangue, from Old Italian aringa (modern Italian arringa) from aringare (“speak in public”) (modern Italian arringare), from aringo (“public assembly”), from Gothic *𐌷𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌲𐍃 (*hriggs) or a compound containing it, akin to Old High German hring (“ring”) (whence German Ring). Doublet of range, rank, ring, and rink.
s: She gave her son a harangue about the dangers of playing in the street.

d: Become productive or fruitful
ety: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French fructefier.
s: He slew the Bull (symbol of the gross Earth which the sunlight fructifies).

d: A simple jointed bit for a horse; without a curb
ety: Apparently from Dutch snavel, from Middle Dutch snavel, snabel (“snout”), diminutive of Middle Dutch snabbe, snebbe (“bird's bill, neb”). Akin to Old Frisian snavel (“mouth”), Middle Low German snabbe (“neb, beak”), Old English nebb (“beak, bill, nose, face”). More at neb.
s: “I shall have to take the mare to-morrow,” said the Tertium Quid, “and she will stand nothing heavier than a snaffle.”

d: Unacceptable behavior (especially ludicrously false statements)
ety: From buncombe, from “speaking to (or for) Buncombe County, North Carolina”, a county in North Carolina named for Edward Buncombe. In 1820, Felix Walker, who represented the county in the U.S. House of Representatives, rose to address the question of admitting Missouri as a free or slave state, his first attempt to speak on the subject after nearly a month of solid debate, right before the vote was
s: The part of that word to focus on is bunk, short for bunkum, which is what these types attack with vigor and all the obsessiveness of the bunkum spreaders themselves.

d: Excited in anticipation
ety: From a- + flutter-.
s: Once inside the house, everything was aflutter until I was safe and sound.

d: Informal terms for personal possessions
ety: British slang from 1941; possibly onomatopoeic of the sound of detonated bombs in the distance.
s: Near-synonyms: clobbering, clubbing, thumping
